p.seg: Now, of all the things that sages and worthies admire,
none is more admirable than intelligence.
(Heaven displays its symbols through the three luminaries;
humans emulate its measure through intelligence.)
Of all the things that intelligence values,
none is more valuable than knowing people.
(Proficiency in writing and calculation
is but one skill among the Six Arts;
insight into people
is the overall responsibility of officials.)
If knowing people is truly wise,
then the talents of the many will find their proper order,
and the endeavors of all achievements will flourish.
Therefore, sages, in creating the lines and images [of the *Yì Jīng*],
established the terms *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) and *xiǎorén* (petty person).
(The *jūnzǐ* is the teacher of the *xiǎorén*,
and the *xiǎorén* is the resource of the *jūnzǐ*;
teachers and resources complement each other;
this has been the case for a long time.)
In composing the *Shī Jīng*,
they distinguished the tasks of differing customs and refined correctness.
(Nine regions have different customs,
and five areas have different habits;
therefore, sages established their teachings without changing their methods,
and formulated their policies without altering their customs.)
In creating ritual and music,
they examined the virtues of the Six Arts and respectful constancy.
(Although they did not change their methods,
they always prioritized poetry and ritual;
although they did not alter their customs,
they always took filial piety and brotherly love as their foundation.)
When facing south [as rulers],
they sought out outstanding and unrestrained talents to assist them.
All of this was done to achieve universal good and complete the work of Heaven.
(Continuing Heaven and completing things is a task of utmost importance.
Therefore, seeking the worthy and promoting the good is always done as if one were falling short.)
Once the work of Heaven is completed,
then all receive praise.
(Loyal ministers exert their strength and demonstrate their abilities;
enlightened rulers obtain the worthy and rest easy;
with loyalty and love between superiors and inferiors,
where can slander and defamation arise?)
Therefore, Yáo 堯 was praised for clearly distinguishing outstanding virtue,
and Shùn 舜 was credited for employing the *èr bā* (twenty-two ministers).
Tāng 湯 was renowned for elevating the worthy from Yǒuxīn 有莘,
and King Wén 文 was esteemed for promoting the old man from the Wèi 渭 River bank.
From this, it can be argued that
in the development of virtue by sages,
who did not exert their intelligence in seeking people
and gain ease in their employment?
(Cǎishì 采士 tending cattle [was found by],
Duke Mù of Qín 秦穆, who thus became hegemon of the western Róng 戎 tribes;
one Zòngfù 仲父 [was found by],
Duke Huán of Qí 齊桓, who thus achieved nine alliances.)
Therefore, though Zhòngní 仲尼 was not tried [in office]
and had no means of promotion,
he still categorized his disciples into four subjects
and broadly discussed people's talents to distinguish three grades.
(He ranked virtue and conduct as the top of the four subjects
and described innate knowledge as the highest of the three grades;
demonstrating virtue and conduct is the gateway to morality,
while having inherent qualities and aspirations is the root of talent and wisdom.)
He also sighed over the *Zhōng Yōng* (Doctrine of the Mean) to highlight the special virtue of sages,
(The virtue of the *Zhōng Yōng*,
is utmost!
People have rarely possessed it for long.
Only sages are capable of it.)
and esteemed virtue to encourage discussion of approximations [to it].
(The son of the Yán 顏 family
is perhaps close to it!
Not deviating from benevolence for three months
is peeking into the door of virtue and conduct.
If it were not for the ambitious and humane nature of those with aspirations,
and they only reached it in days and months,
how could they ever achieve it?)
He taught the six obscurations to warn against the failings of biased talents.
(The benevolent love things,
but are obscured by indecisiveness;
the trustworthy reveal sincerity,
but are obscured by lack of concealment.
These are common failings of biased talents.)
He considered the *kuáng* (zealous) and *juàn* (cautious) to accommodate talents who were either constrained or resistant.
(Some advance towards morality,
while others purify themselves and do nothing.
Those in positions of authority should accommodate both of their abilities,
so that the constrained and resistant are both utilized.)
He detested emptiness and lack of trustworthiness,
to show that what appears to be [something] is difficult to maintain.
(A thick face and deep emotions are difficult even for sages to discern.
Listen to their words and observe their actions,
then the appearance of trustworthiness will have no escape.)
He also said, "Examine what they are comfortable with,
observe what they follow,"
to know their conduct in dwelling and stopping.
(Their words must match the beginning to reach the end,
and their actions must be observed from the start to seek completion,
then their inner and outer feelings can be roughly observed.)
The examination of people's character
is thus so detailed.
(Without detailed examination, the ranks of officials will lose their order,
and the endeavors of all administration will be abandoned.)
Therefore, I dare to rely on the teachings of the sages,
aspiring to write an account of people's character,
hoping to supplement what has been forgotten.
May learned gentlemen examine its meaning.
Chapter One: Nine Manifestations
(People's emotions and natures,
and aspirations are different.
Manifesting spirit and observing appearance,
there are nine verifications of form.)
"Jiǔ Zhēng" (Nine Evidences) – Chapter 1
Generally, the foundation of people and things
comes from qíngxìng (情性).
(Xìngzhì (性質) is endowed by nature,
while qíng (情) changes due to acquired habits.
Therefore, when observing people and examining things,
one should seek their xìngzhì (性質).)
The principles of qíngxìng (情性)
are extremely subtle and profound.
If not for the insight of sages,
who could possibly understand them?
(Knowledge has no form or shape,
so ordinary people cannot perceive it;
only sages can witness it directly and illuminate it.)
All beings with blood and breath
invariably contain yuányī (元一) as their essence.
(If the essence is not complete, they cannot withstand cold and heat
and endure the four seasons.)
They receive yīn (陰) and yáng (陽) to establish their xìng (性).
(Xìng (性) is based on yīn (陰) and yáng (陽),
so the meanings of firmness and gentleness are distinct.)
They embody the wǔxíng (五行) to manifest their form.
(Strong bones and flexible tendons
both derive their essence from metal and wood.)
If there is form and substance,
it is still possible to approach and seek it.
(Because qi (氣) and sè (色) are manifested externally,
those who judge appearances can understand their true nature.)
Of all the qualities of a person,
moderation and harmony are the most valued.
(A pure substance readily accepts color,
and a sweet taste readily accepts blending.
Moderation and harmony
are the foundation of all virtuous conduct
and the fertile ground of human emotions.)
The quality of moderation and harmony
must be plain and without strong flavor,
(Only with plainness
can the five flavors be harmonized.
If it is bitter,
it cannot become sweet;
if it is sour,
it cannot become salty.)
Therefore, it can blend the five elements,
and change in response to the seasons.
(With plainness and impartiality,
all materials will be managed;
when applied there will be suitability;
and adaptation to change will be without obstruction.)
Therefore, when observing a person and assessing their qualities,
one must first observe their plainness,
and then seek their intelligence.
(Like the Jìlù horse,
though outstanding and surpassing the crowd,
if its temperament is not harmonious,
it will inevitably suffer the misfortune of ruining its bit, smashing its head, and tearing its chest.)
Intelligence
is the essence of Yīn and Yáng.
(Lí represents the eyes, Kǎn represents the ears,
from which seeing and hearing arise.)
When Yīn and Yáng are clear and harmonious,
there will be inner wisdom and outer brightness.
The sage is purely radiant,
able to combine both beauties.
Knowing the subtle and understanding the obvious,
(both the ears and eyes are used to observe,
penetrating the hidden and reaching the subtle,
officials are assigned positions and materials are given direction,
nothing is missed in undertakings.)
Apart from sages,
no one can fully achieve both.
(Although one may gain through the eyes,
one may lose through the ears.)
Therefore, a person of clarity
understands the mechanisms of action,
but is ignorant of profound considerations;
(skilled in advancing,
but ignorant of stopping and being still.
Using them to advance,
they will desire speed and become hasty;
using them to contemplate deeply,
they will resist and not penetrate.)
A person of profound consideration
understands the source of stillness,
but is hindered by speed and agility.
(Their nature is peaceful and silent,
and their wisdom lacks responsiveness.
Using them for leisure and quiet,
the way of profound subtlety can be constructed;
using them to aid the world,
they will be forceful and quick, but without accomplishment.)
It is like fire and the sun, shining outwards,
unable to see inward;
metal and water reflect inwards,
unable to shine outwards.
(People each have their abilities,
and things each have their nature.
Therefore, the sage employs those of clarity to advance and act,
and entrusts those of profound consideration to maintain and preserve,
and then movement and stillness are in accordance with the seasons,
and engagement and withdrawal are appropriate.)
The meaning of these two
is, in essence, the difference between Yīn and Yáng.
(Yáng moves and Yīn is still,
which is the fixed nature of Heaven and Earth,
let alone people and things?)
If we were to assess their material quality,
and examine the Five Materials,
the manifestations of the Five Materials
would also be evident in their physical form.
(The spirit (qì) of xiāo-yǒng (䈥勇) has a bluish hue,
the spirit (qì) of xuè-yǒng (血勇) has a reddish hue;
internal movement and external form
how can they be concealed?)
As for their presence in the body,
wood is bone (gǔ), metal is xiāo (䈥), fire is qì (氣), earth is muscle (jī), and water is blood (xuè)—
these are the images of the Five Materials.
(The Five Natures
are the means of forming shapes.
The Five Materials are the mother
hence, qì (氣) and color follow and are complete.)
The essence of the Five Materials
each has something to provide.
The Five Natures are different;
each has something it receives.
Those who receive more of a certain nature will give rise to a biased nature.
Therefore, bones that are upright yet flexible
are called hóng-yì (弘毅);
hóng-yì (弘毅)
is the substance of rén (仁).
Wood provides shade and shelter,
being the substance of rén (仁).
If the substance is not hóng-yì (弘毅),
one cannot achieve rén (仁).
Qì (氣) that is clear and bright
is called wén-lǐ (文理);
wén-lǐ (文理)
is the foundation of lǐ (禮).
Fire illuminates and discerns,
being the foundation of lǐ (禮).
If the foundation lacks wén-lǐ (文理),
one cannot achieve lǐ (禮).
A body that is upright and solid
is called zhēn-gù (貞固);
zhēn-gù (貞固)
is the basis of xìn (信).
Earth necessarily brings forth and gives life,
being the basis of xìn (信).
If the basis is not zhēn-gù (貞固),
one cannot achieve xìn (信).
Xiāo (䈥) that is strong and refined
is called yǒng-gǎn (勇敢);
yǒng-gǎn (勇敢)
is the decisiveness of yì (義).
Metal can sever and cut,
being the decisiveness of yì (義).
If decisiveness is not yǒng-gǎn (勇敢),
one cannot achieve yì (義).
Color that is balanced and smooth
is called tōng-wēi (通微);
tōng-wēi (通微)
is the source of zhì (智).
Water flows and penetrates,
being the source of zhì (智).
If the source is not tōng-wēi (通微),
one cannot achieve zhì (智).
The Five Substances are constant in nature;
therefore, they are called the Five Constants.
The Five Materials
are the constant qì (氣) of Heaven and Earth;
the Five Virtues
are the constant conduct of humans and things.
The differences in the Five Constants
are listed as the Five Virtues:
therefore, warmth and uprightness with gentleness and resoluteness are
the virtue of wood;
warmth without uprightness is weakness,
and gentleness without resoluteness is timidity.
Firm strength with breadth and resoluteness are
the virtue of metal;
strength without firmness is decisiveness,
and breadth without resoluteness is deficiency.
Sincerity and reverence with order and respect are
the virtue of water;
sincerity without reverence is disobedience,
and order without respect is chaos.
Generosity and prudence with gentleness and uprightness are
the virtue of earth;
generosity without prudence is negligence,
and gentleness without uprightness is dispersion.
Simplicity and fluency with clarity and penetration are
the virtue of fire.
Simplicity without fluency is stagnation,
and clarity without penetration is obscurity.
Although bodily transformations are infinite,
they still depend on these five qualities.
Human emotions are ever-changing,
impossible to fully grasp.
Seeking their common origin,
it always lies within these five.
Therefore, the signs of firmness, gentleness, clarity, fluency, integrity, and steadfastness
are evident in appearance,
seen in voice and expression,
and revealed in emotions and taste,
each according to its own image.
It is a natural principle
that the spirit moves form and expression.
When sincerity arises from within,
virtue radiates outward.
Therefore, when the heart is of bright and upright quality,
its bearing is strong and steadfast;
when the heart is of excellent and decisive quality,
its bearing is advancing and fierce;
when the heart is of balanced and orderly quality,
its bearing is peaceful and leisurely.
Thus, movements of bearing create appearance,
each having its own manner:
the movement of an upright appearance
is lofty and proper;
the movement of an excellent appearance
is cautious and respectful;
the movement of a virtuous appearance
is dignified and respectful.
The demeanor of a person,
originates from the heart and *qì*;
the heart and *qì* are within,
the demeanor is seen without.
The manifestation of heart and *qì*,
is the change in voice.
When the heart is not fixated on one thing,
the voice is harmonious and yet changing.
*Qì* combines to form sound,
sound corresponds to *lǜ lǚ*:
that which is clear and bright is *lǜ*,
that which is harmonious and even is *lǚ*.
There is the sound of harmony and evenness,
there is the sound of clarity and smoothness,
there is the sound of echoing and spreading.
The heart and *qì* are different,
therefore the sound emitted is also different.
When the sound flows smoothly with the *qì*,
then substance exists within appearance:
without *qì* there is no way to form sound,
when sound is formed, appearance responds.
Therefore, true benevolence
must have a gentle countenance;
true courage
must have an assertive and striving countenance;
true wisdom
must have a clear and perceptive countenance.
Since the sounds are distinct,
the countenances are also of different forms.
The countenance is seen in the appearance,
this is what is called manifesting spirit (*zhēng shén*).
The slowness or quickness of the appearance,
is the proof of the spirit.
When the spirit is manifested in the appearance,
then emotions are expressed in the eyes.
The eyes are the envoys of the heart,
therefore they respond to the heart and express it.
Therefore, benevolence,
the essence of the eyes,
is sincere and upright;
if the heart does not lean or rely,
then the gaze will not be shifty or perverse.
Courage,
the essence of the gall,
is radiant and strong.
If the will is not timid,
then the gaze will not be withered.
However, these are all talents leaning to one extreme,
taking overpowering the body as their substance.
They cannot be stern without anger,
authoritative without rage.
Therefore, if overpowering substance is not refined,
then their affairs will not succeed.
Able to be courageous but not able to be timid,
actions will inevitably be followed by regret and distress.
Therefore, being straight without being yielding is like wood;
wood is strong and attacks shortcomings,
losing its straightness.
Being tough without being refined is like strength;
lifting the cauldron results in broken kneecaps,
losing its true strength.
Being firm without being upright is like foolishness;
being stubborn and self-righteous,
leads to foolishness and obstinacy.
Being full of *qì* without clarity is like transgressing;
words are unclear and not smooth,
expressions transgress and achieve nothing.
Being smooth without being even is like being dissolute.
Loving wisdom without limits,
results in dissipating and breaking ties.
Therefore, the substance of moderation and balance,
is different from these kinds.
Courageous yet able to be timid,
benevolent yet able to make decisions,
their substance combines both,
therefore they are the masters of all talents.
The five constants being complete,
wrapped with a bland taste.
Having the measure of both saltiness and sourness,
yet taking tastelessness as control.
The five substances are full within,
the five essences are manifest without.
The five substances are subtly condensed,
pure and radiant outward.
Therefore, the color of the eyes is the light of the five luminaries.
The heart is clear and the eyes are bright,
brilliantly self-illuminating.
Therefore it is said, "Things are born with form,
form has spirit and essence."
Without asking about the wise or the foolish,
all receive the endowment of *qì* and substance, the nature of *yīn yáng*,
only wisdom has refinement and coarseness,
form has shallowness and depth.
Seek their refined color,
observe their appearance and form,
down to the servants and herdsmen,
all can be imagined and understood.
To know the spirit,
is to exhaust principle and fulfill nature.
The sages have a way to see the movements of the world and to imitate them in form,
therefore they are able to exhaust principle and fulfill nature to the point of destiny.
The complete expression of one's nature is manifested in the
nine characteristics.
Yīnyáng generate each other,
and the numbers do not exceed nine.
Therefore, changes in disposition and feelings,
are similarly reflected in one's inherent qualities.
Thus, the quality of evenness or unevenness lies in the *shén*;
the *shén*
is the master of one's inherent qualities.
Therefore, if the *shén* is even, then the qualities are even;
if the *shén* is uneven, then the qualities are uneven.
Clarity or obscurity resides in the *jīng*;
the *jīng*
is the foundation of reality.
Therefore, if the *jīng* is wise, then reality is clear;
if the *jīng* is turbid, then reality is obscure.
Courage or cowardice lies in the *qià*;
the *qià*
is the application of power.
Therefore, if the *qià* is strong, then the power is courageous;
if the *qià* is weak, then the power is cowardly.
Strength or weakness is rooted in the bones;
bones
are the foundation of one's constitution.
Therefore, if the bones are strong, then the constitution is strong;
if the bones are weak, then the constitution is weak.
Agitation or calmness is determined by the *qì*;
the *qì*
is the ground for decision.
Abundant *qì* leads to agitation;
harmonious *qì* leads to calmness.
Sadness or joy is expressed in one's countenance;
one's countenance
is the indicator of one's emotions.
Therefore, a sorrowful countenance arises from sad emotions;
a joyful countenance arises from joyful emotions.
Decline or uprightness is reflected in one's bearing;
one's bearing
is the outward manifestation of one's form.
Therefore, a declining bearing arises from a failing form;
an upright bearing arises from a respectful form.
Agitation or composure is expressed in one's appearance;
one's appearance
is the symbol of one's behavior.
Therefore, improper behavior results in agitated appearance;
proper behavior results in composed appearance.
Haste or slowness is manifested in one's speech.
Speech
is the expression of one's heart.
Therefore, a generous heart leads to slow speech;
a narrow heart leads to hasty speech.
As for the person who
is simple and plain in quality,
wise within and bright without,
with strong *qià* and firm constitution,
clear in voice and joyful in countenance,
with noble bearing and upright appearance,
then all nine characteristics will be present,
and he will possess pure virtue.
If not a person of supreme virtue and great stature,
who else could attain this?
If any of the nine characteristics are violated,
such violation indicates perversity.
Then he is a person of mixed and imperfect talent.
Perhaps his voice is clear and his countenance joyful,
but his quality is not simple and plain;
or perhaps his *qià* is strong and his constitution firm,
but his bearing is not noble and upright.
If these three aspects differ,
their virtue is described differently.
Those with singular talent are named for their one excellence,
those with multiple talents are classified by their virtuous qualities,
and those with multiple virtues embody the principle of the Mean.
Therefore, people with singular talent
are named after their specific ability,
just as the many artisans and craftsmen
each have their own title.
People with multiple talents
are classified by their virtues;
*rén*, *yì*, *lǐ*, and *zhì*
are each considered one aspect of their virtue.
People with multiple virtues
are given even more beautiful epithets.
The *Dào* cannot be described by a single attribute,
and virtue cannot be confined to one aspect.
It nurtures all things without being called *rén*,
and it harmonizes all forms without being called virtue.
It is serene, simple, and plain,
existing without boundary with all things;
who can know its name?
Therefore, one who possesses multiple virtues
is said to embody the Mean;
dwelling in the center and acting according to the norm,
hence it is called the Mean.
The Mean
is the standard of the sage.
Great *rén* cannot be approached,
great *yì* cannot be repaid,
and to praise someone without virtue
is to attribute his name to the sages.
To embody it in a complete but subtle form
is called virtue and conduct;
virtue and conduct
are praised in the *Dà Yǎ*.
To practice *rén* to cherish things,
to establish *yì* to benefit *rén*,
to lose the *Dào* and achieve virtue,
this is still second best.
A single excellence is called a singular talent,
a singular talent
is the quality of the *Xiǎo Yǎ*;
to have only *rén* without *yì*,
or only *yì* without *rén*,
is to fail to achieve comprehensive benefit,
each adhering to only one path,
thus their name does not reach the level of the *Dà Yǎ*.
A single characteristic is called a semblance,
a semblance
is a type of corrupted virtue;
pure denunciation resembles honesty but is not honesty,
pure licentiousness resembles understanding but is not understanding.
One excellence and one defect is called mixed;
mixed
refers to a person without constancy.
Good and evil are mixed together,
and the heart has no fixed principle.
Such lack of constancy,
how can it be assessed?
Those without constancy or those who merely resemble virtue
are all the lowest of the *Fēng* poems.
Those whose hearts are extremely hardened
are beyond the reach of education and transformation.
The qualities of the lowest of the low
cannot be fully discussed,
therefore they are briefly mentioned without detail.
They gather into flocks and form groups;
how can they be counted?
Chapter Two: Distinctions in Physical Form
Receiving the *qì* of *yīn* and *yáng*,
personalities possess strength and gentleness.
Restrained resistance, elegance and simplicity,
physical forms increasingly become distinct.
Section 2: On Distinctions in Form (〈Tǐ Bié〉Dì Èr)
Now, the virtue of Zhōngyōng
has a substance without a name.
It is expansive and not tied to one appearance;
people have no way to describe it.
Therefore, being salty without being overly salty,
can it be called salty?
It tolerates no excess of saltiness;
it achieves the perfection of all salts, being the same as saltiness.
Being bland without being excessively bland,
can it be called bland?
Its flavor does not revert to excessive blandness.
Being plain without being coarse,
can it be called plain?
Its principle is not coarsely simple.
Being refined without being ornamented,
can it be called refined?
Its colors are not painted with ornamentation.
It can be awe-inspiring and cherishing,
can be discerning and reserved,
residing in the harmony of saltiness and blandness,
dwelling in the juncture of plainness and refinement.
Therefore, when viewed from afar, it is dignified;
when approached, it is refined.
Its words fill the world without being verbose.
It changes without fixed direction,
using comprehension as its principle.
It adapts to changes and suits transformations,
aiming to understand all things.
Therefore, those who are inflexible exceed it;
they are fiercely rigid and strive on the path of advancement.
And those who are constrained do not attain it;
they are inertly inactive outside of rigidity and inflexibility.
Indeed, being constrained and resisting deviates from the mean,
therefore strengths are highlighted,
but principles are also lost.
If one nourishes the body to an extreme,
then tigers will devour its exterior;
if a high gate hangs thinly,
then illness will attack its interior.
Therefore, those who are strict, upright, firm, and resolute,
their talent lies in correction,
but their fault lies in fault-finding and accusation;
accusation arises from strictness and severity.
Those who are gentle, compliant, peaceful, and forgiving,
their strength lies in tolerance,
but their fault lies in indecisiveness;
excessive doubt arises from gentleness and timidity.
Those who are heroic, fierce, outstanding, and strong,
their duty lies in courage and intensity,
but their fault lies in excessive suspicion;
disregard for the law arises from wildness and ferocity.
Those who are refined, excellent, fearful, and cautious,
their strength lies in respect and carefulness,
but their fault lies in excessive doubt;
difficulty in making decisions arises from fear and caution.
Those who are strong, upright, firm, and resolute,
their use lies in being pillars and supports,
but their fault lies in being stubborn and inflexible;
insistence on one's own way arises from firmness and resoluteness.
Those who are skilled at discussion, argumentation, and reasoning,
their ability lies in resolving knots,
but their fault lies in being unrestrained and digressive;
arrogance and digression arise from cleverness in argumentation.
Those who are broadly learned, universally knowledgeable, comprehensive, and harmonious,
their greatness lies in covering and enriching,
but their fault lies in being mixed and impure;
being mixed and impure arises from universal knowledge.
Those who are pure, aloof, honest, and clean,
their virtue lies in frugality and firmness,
but their fault lies in being confined and narrow;
being confined and narrow arises from honesty and cleanliness.
Those who are leisurely, active, open, and straightforward,
their achievement lies in climbing and ascending,
but their fault lies in being distant and surpassing;
being distant and surpassing arises from being open and straightforward.
Those who are deep, quiet, secretive, and subtle,
their essence lies in profundity and subtlety,
but their fault lies in being slow and procrastinating;
being slow and procrastinating arises from being deep and quiet.
Those who are simple, exposed, direct, and thorough,
their quality lies in being centered and sincere,
but their fault lies in not being subtle;
leaking and exposing arises from being direct and thorough.
Those who are highly intelligent and conceal their feelings,
their power lies in deception and strategy,
but their fault lies in being hesitant and indecisive;
concealment and deviation arise from concealing feelings.
As for those whose progress in virtue never ceases,
measure the Mean to guard against the constraints and resistance of their talents,
the resistant ones will thereby strive and exert themselves,
and the constrained ones will thereby guard their limits.
But if you point out people’s shortcomings to increase their faults,
the constrained will become more constrained,
and the resistant will become more resistant.

Chapter 5: Cáinéng (Talent and Ability)

I think this is a misnomer.
Talented individuals are like vessels,
differing in size.
To use a large cauldron being unable to cook a chicken
as an analogy for great talent being unable to manage small matters
misses the mark.
The term "capability"
is already a definitive attribute.
First, there is a defined quality,
and then the name of capability arises.
How can there be someone capable in great matters but not in small ones?
All that is called "capable in great matters but not in small ones"
stems from differences in the temperament of being broad or narrow.
The broad are expansive and generous,
the narrow are pressing and urgent.
Temperament has broadness and narrowness,
hence suitability varies in size.
Broad generosity is suitable for governing the large,
pressing urgency is suitable for governing the small.
Broad and generous people
are suitable for governing commanderies and states,
allowing subordinates to exert their skills
and collectively accomplish their tasks;
pressing urgency leads to troublesome details,
and affairs fail.
Pressing and urgent people
are suitable for managing a hundred *lǐ*,
ensuring matters are handled personally.
Broad generosity results in laxity,
and affairs are neglected.
Thus, commanderies and counties
are different in the size of their structures.
If one can govern a large commandery well,
then one can govern a small commandery well;
if one can govern a large county well,
one can also govern a small county well.
If one discusses and distinguishes based on the reality of breadth and urgency,
then one should speak of different suitabilities based on size,
and not say that one is capable in great matters but not in small ones.
If one is capable in great matters but not in small ones,
wouldn't Zhòng Ní 仲尼 have been unable to serve as a retainer for the Jì Shì 季氏 family?
Furthermore, chickens and oxen
also differ in the size of their structures,
a cauldron that can cook an ox
can also cook a chicken;
a saucepan that can cook a chicken
cannot cook a calf.
Therefore, cauldrons should also vary in size.
If one is able to cook a calf,
then how could one not be able to cook a chicken?
There is only suitability and unsuitability,
how can there be capability and incapability?
Therefore, one who can govern a large commandery
can also govern a small commandery.
Extrapolating from this argument,

not just in terms of size.

Chapter Nine: Eight Observations
The Eight Observations:
First, observe their taking and giving to clarify what is mixed within.

Second, observe their reactions to changes to assess their normal behavior.

then their normal behavior can be assessed.
Third, observe their ultimate nature to understand their reputation.

seeing their countenance, you will know their name.
Fourth, observe their motivations to distinguish between reliance and semblance.
Reliance on accusation resembles uprightness;
in haste, it is difficult to discern.
Observe where they find comfort;
it will be clearly distinguishable.
Fifth, observe their love and respect to know their openness and obstructiveness.
Pure love means things are close and emotions flow;
pure respect means principles are distant and emotions are obstructed.
Sixth, observe their emotional mechanisms to distinguish between forgiveness and confusion.
Getting what they desire leads to forgiveness;
violating what they desire leads to confusion.
Seventh, observe their shortcomings to know their strengths.
Though accusation and criticism are shortcomings,
their strength lies in being straightforward.

if the talent is not intelligent,
